A computer system has four main parts: input, the CPU, memory and output. Data goes in through the input, the CPU processes it, memory holds data and instructions, and the result comes out through the output.

lessons.title: Short Questions — with Answers
lessons.notes_html:
4. What is the difference between hardware and software?

Hardware is the physical part of a computer system that you can see and touch, such as the keyboard, monitor, CPU and printer. Software is the set of programs and instructions that tell the hardware what to do; it cannot be touched. Hardware without software is useless, and software cannot run without hardware. Together they form a working computer system.

5. What is Information Technology? Describe it in detail.

Information Technology (IT) is the technology that merges computing with high-speed communication links to carry data in the form of text, sound, images and video from place to place over the global village. It allows data stored or processed on computers to be shared and exchanged almost as if users were sitting face to face. IT covers hardware, software, networks and communication systems, and it is used in education, medicine, business, research and daily life.

6. What is implementation? Describe its approaches.

Implementation is the stage of the system development life cycle in which the new system is actually put into use after testing. Its approaches are: direct implementation, in which the old system is replaced at once; parallel implementation, in which the old and new systems run together for a time; and phased implementation, in which the new system is introduced in parts. Each approach balances risk, cost and the time needed for users to adjust.

7. What is the usage of an input device? List a few of them.

An input device is used to enter data and instructions into the computer so that the CPU can process them. Common input devices are the keyboard, mouse, joystick, trackball, scanner, light pen, digital camera, microphone and optical mark reader (OMR). Each device converts a different form of data, such as typing, pointing, pictures or sound, into a form the computer can use.

8. Describe the enhanced keyboard and its segments.

The enhanced keyboard is the standard keyboard with 101 or more keys, arranged for fast and comfortable typing. Its segments are the typewriter keys (letters, digits and punctuation), the function keys (F1 to F12) used for shortcuts, the numeric keypad for quick number entry, the cursor-control and navigation keys (arrows, Home, End, Page Up, Page Down), and special keys such as Ctrl, Alt, Esc and Enter. The QWERTY arrangement is the standard layout of its letter keys.

9. Write the name of the input device that can control the cursor movement.

The mouse is the main input device used to control the movement of the cursor (pointer) on the screen. Moving the mouse on a flat surface moves the pointer, and its buttons are used to select, open and drag objects. The joystick and the trackball can also control cursor movement, but the mouse is the standard pointing device for this purpose.

10. What is the function of an output device? List a few of them.

An output device is used to present the processed result of the computer to the user in a usable form, such as on screen or on paper. Common output devices are the monitor (VDU), printer, plotter, speaker and headphone. The monitor gives soft copy output on the screen, while the printer and plotter give hard copy output on paper.

11. Describe the functioning of a Laser printer.

A laser printer is a non-impact printer that prints a whole page at a time with high speed and fine quality. A laser beam draws the image of the page on a light-sensitive drum, toner powder sticks to the charged parts of the drum, and the toner is then transferred to paper and fixed by heat. Because nothing strikes the paper, laser printing is quiet, and it is widely used for sharp text and graphics.

12. What is the usage of a plotter? Name its different kinds.

A plotter is an output device used to draw large, accurate graphics such as engineering drawings, maps, building plans and charts, which ordinary printers cannot draw well. Its different kinds are the drum plotter, in which the paper moves on a rotating drum, and the flatbed plotter, in which the paper stays flat on a table while the pen moves over it.

13. Define the term 'Operating System' in your own words.

An operating system is the system software that manages all the resources of a computer and acts as a link between the user and the hardware. It controls the CPU, memory, input and output devices and files, and it provides the platform on which application programs run. Without an operating system, the user could not run programs or use the hardware easily.

14. Describe the function of the following input devices: (i) Mouse (ii) Joystick (iii) Trackball (iv) Scanner (v) Light Pen (vi) Digital Camera.

(i) Mouse: controls the cursor and selects objects by pointing, clicking and dragging. (ii) Joystick: controls movement, mainly in games and simulators, by tilting a stick. (iii) Trackball: controls the cursor by rotating a ball held in a fixed base; it is popular with laptop users. (iv) Scanner: copies pictures, text and documents into the computer as digital images. (v) Light Pen: points directly at the screen to select or draw. (vi) Digital Camera: captures still pictures and video directly in digital form for the computer.

15. What do you understand by 'SDLC'? Define its steps properly.

SDLC means System Development Life Cycle: the series of steps used to build a working information system. Its steps are: (1) Problem definition, stating what the system must do; (2) Feasibility study, checking whether the system is possible and worthwhile; (3) System analysis, studying the present system and the user's needs; (4) System design, planning inputs, outputs, files and programs; (5) Coding, writing the programs; (6) Testing, checking the system for errors; (7) Implementation, putting the new system into use; and (8) Maintenance, improving the system and removing problems reported by users.

lessons.notes_html:
4. What is the difference between LAN and WAN?

A LAN (Local Area Network) connects computers within a small area such as one building, office or campus, at high speed and low cost. A WAN (Wide Area Network) connects computers over a large area, such as cities or countries, using telephone lines, microwaves or satellites, and it is slower and more expensive than a LAN. In short, LAN is local and fast, while WAN is wide-area and long-distance.

5. What method does an Ethernet network use to control access to the network?

An Ethernet network controls access by the CSMA/CD method: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection. Each computer first listens to the cable; if the cable is free it sends its data, and if two computers send at the same time and a collision occurs, both stop, wait a random time, and try again. This sharing rule lets many computers use the same cable without a central controller.

6. What is Topology? Describe the types of topology.

Topology is the physical arrangement or layout by which computers are connected in a network. Its main types are: bus topology, where all computers share one central cable; ring topology, where computers are joined in a closed ring; star topology, where every computer is connected to a central hub; mesh topology, where computers are directly connected to each other; and tree topology, which combines bus and star layouts in a hierarchy.

7. What is WWW?

WWW stands for World Wide Web: the system of linked documents and resources on the internet that are viewed with a web browser. Each document, called a web page, is held on a web server and is reached by its address (URL), and pages are linked to each other by hyperlinks. The Web lets users read, search and share text, pictures, sound and video around the world.

8. Describe the OSI Model and types of layers of OSI Model.

The OSI model is a seven-layer standard that describes how data moves from one computer to another over a network. Its layers, from top to bottom, are: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link and Physical. Each layer performs one part of the job, such as addressing, routing, error control and the physical transmission of bits, so that different systems can communicate with each other.

9. Difference between Intranet and Extranet.

An intranet is a private network inside one organisation that uses internet technology but is open only to its own staff, for sharing internal information. An extranet is an extension of an intranet that also gives controlled access to selected outsiders, such as business partners or customers. So an intranet serves insiders only, while an extranet serves insiders plus trusted outsiders.

10. Difference between FTP and HTTP.

FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is used to transfer complete files between computers over the internet, such as uploading and downloading files. HTTP (Hyper Text Transfer Protocol) is used to transfer web pages, with their text, images and links, from a web server to a web browser. In short, FTP moves files, while HTTP moves web pages for viewing.

11. Define the gateway and router.

A gateway is a device or program that connects two different types of networks and translates data between them so that they can communicate. A router is a device that connects networks of the same or similar type and forwards data packets along the best path towards their destination. The gateway translates between different systems, while the router directs traffic between networks.

12. Define the term 'Operating System' in your own words.

An operating system is the system software that manages the computer's hardware and provides the base on which all other programs run. It controls the processor, memory, storage and input/output devices, manages files, and gives the user a way to run programs. Common examples are Windows and Linux.

13. Describe the function of (i) Dedicated Server Network (ii) Peer-to-Peer Network.

(i) Dedicated Server Network: one powerful computer, the server, is set aside to provide services such as files and printing to the other computers (clients); it gives central control and security. (ii) Peer-to-Peer Network: all computers are equal and share their resources directly with each other, with no dedicated server; it is simple and cheap for small networks but harder to control and secure.

lessons.notes_html:
4. What is data communication? Define the basic components of a communication network.

Data communication is the transfer of data or information from one place to another through a communication channel, such as a cable or wireless link. Its five basic components are: the message (the data to be sent); the sender (the device that sends it); the receiver (the device that receives it); the communication channel (the path, such as twisted pair, coaxial cable or fiber optic); and the encoder/decoder, which converts the message into a form fit for the channel and back again.

5. Define the modem and its types.

A modem is a device that converts digital signals from a computer into analog signals for transmission over telephone lines (modulation), and converts received analog signals back into digital form (demodulation). Its types are the internal modem, fitted inside the system unit as a circuit board, and the external modem, connected outside the computer as a separate box.

6. Differentiate between Asynchronous and Synchronous transmission.

In asynchronous transmission, data are sent one character at a time, with a start bit before and a stop bit after each character, so the receiver can resynchronise on every character; it is simple but slower. In synchronous transmission, data are sent as a continuous block of characters controlled by a common clock, with no start and stop bits on each character; it is faster and is used for large volumes of data, but it needs more expensive equipment.

Start and stop bitsStart bit before and stop bit after each characterNo start and stop bits on each character
TimingReceiver resynchronises on every characterControlled by a common clock

EquipmentSimpleMore expensive equipment needed

7. Briefly explain the various communication media.

Communication media are the paths that carry data. Guided media carry signals along a physical path: twisted pair cable (ordinary telephone wire), coaxial cable (a central copper wire with shielding, used for cable TV and networks) and fiber-optic cable (thin glass strands carrying pulses of light, very fast and free from interference). Unguided media carry signals through the air or space without a wire: microwaves, radio waves, infrared and satellites.

8. Define the Modem.

A modem (modulator-demodulator) is a communication device that lets a computer send and receive data over telephone lines. It modulates, that is, converts the computer's digital signals into analog signals for sending, and demodulates, that is, converts incoming analog signals back into digital signals the computer can use.

9. What is bandwidth? Explain bandwidth briefly.

Bandwidth is the capacity of a communication channel: the range of frequencies it can carry, or the amount of data it can transmit in a given time. A channel with greater bandwidth can carry more data at once and at higher speed. For example, a voice telephone channel has a narrow bandwidth, while a broadband channel used for high-speed data has a much wider bandwidth.

10. Differentiate between guided media and unguided media.

Guided media, also called bounded media, guide signals along a fixed physical path, such as twisted pair, coaxial cable or fiber-optic cable; they are protected from outside interference but must be laid down. Unguided media, also called unbounded media, send signals through the air or space, such as microwaves, radio waves and satellites; they need no cabling and cover long distances, but they can suffer from interference and weather.

5. Explain the term Computer Aided Manufacturing process.

Computer Aided Manufacturing (CAM) is the use of computers to control and manage the manufacturing process in a factory. The computer directs machines and robots that cut, shape, assemble and test products, following a design stored in the system. CAM gives accurate, fast and repeated production with less waste, and it is widely used in automobile, textile and electronics industries.

6. What is meant by computer simulation?

Computer simulation means using a computer to imitate a real process or system so that it can be studied without doing the real thing. The computer follows a model of the real system and shows what would happen under different conditions. Simulations are used to train pilots, test new cars and aeroplanes, predict weather and study scientific problems that would be dangerous or expensive to test in reality.

7. What is an ATM?

An ATM (Automated Teller Machine) is a computerised banking machine that lets customers obtain cash and carry out banking services at any time, without going inside a bank. By inserting a bank card and entering a personal identification number (PIN), a customer can withdraw cash, check the account balance and get a mini statement. ATMs are the best-known face of electronic banking.

8. Explain how computer can be useful in business.

Computers help business by keeping records of sales, stock, customers and accounts quickly and accurately. They prepare bills, payrolls and reports, support electronic shopping and banking, and let offices communicate by e-mail and video conferencing. With fast and reliable information, managers can take better decisions, serve customers faster and reduce the cost of routine work.

9. Explain how computer can be useful in medical field.

In the medical field, computers keep patients' records, help doctors diagnose disease, and control laboratory tests and scanning machines such as CAT (Computerised Axial Topography) scanners, which build detailed pictures of the inside of the body. Computers also support surgery, monitor patients in intensive care, manage hospitals and pharmacies, and let doctors consult specialists far away.

10. Define the role of E-Commerce in our daily life.

E-Commerce means buying and selling goods and services over the internet. In daily life it lets people shop from home at any hour, compare prices, pay electronically and have goods delivered to their door, through e-shops and online banking. It saves time and travel, gives a wider choice than local shops, and lets even small businesses sell to customers across the country and the world.

11. How computer can be useful in weather forecasting?

For weather forecasting, computers collect accurate data from weather stations, satellites and radars all over the world, and then process this huge amount of data with mathematical models of the atmosphere. The results are forecast maps showing rain, wind, storms and temperature for the coming days. Because the calculations are enormous, only fast computers can produce forecasts in time to warn people about severe weather.

12. Define the CBT training.

CBT (Computer Based Training) is training given through a computer instead of a classroom teacher. The learner works through lessons, exercises, pictures and tests on the computer, at his own speed and whenever he has time. CBT is used to train employees, teach driving, and give technical courses, because one program can train many people in different places at the same cost.

13. Describe the online shopping and banking.

Online shopping means buying goods through websites: the customer selects items in an e-shop, pays by card or electronic transfer, and the goods are delivered to his home. Online banking means using the internet or an ATM to use bank services, such as checking balances, transferring money and paying bills, without visiting a branch. Both save time, work day and night, and need care about passwords and security.

14. Define the Videoconferencing.

Videoconferencing is a form of conferencing in which people in different places can see and hear each other at the same time over a network, using video cameras, microphones, speakers and screens. It is an advanced form of teleconferencing. It saves travel time and cost, and it is used for business meetings, distance teaching, medical consultation and interviews.

lessons.notes_html:
4. What is CPU? Describe briefly.

The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is the brain of the computer: the hardware unit that carries out instructions and controls the whole system. It has three main parts: the Control Unit, which fetches and decodes instructions; the ALU (Arithmetic and Logic Unit), which performs calculations and comparisons; and the registers, small high-speed storage places inside the CPU that hold data and addresses during processing. The CPU works together with memory through buses.

5. Explain the architecture of computer system.

The architecture of a computer system is the organisation of its main parts and how they are connected. The CPU (Control Unit, ALU and registers) is joined by buses to the main memory (RAM and ROM) and to input and output devices through ports and controllers. Data and instructions travel on the data bus, addresses on the address bus, and control signals on the control bus. Secondary storage, such as hard disks, holds data and programs when they are not in use.

6. Differentiate between the following: (i) PROM and EPROM (ii) Address Bus and Control Bus (iii) Serial and Parallel Ports (iv) Linker and Loader (v) CU and ALU.

(i) PROM (Programmable Read Only Memory) can be programmed once and cannot be changed; EPROM (Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory) can be erased with ultraviolet light and programmed again. (ii) The address bus carries the address of the memory location to be used; the control bus carries control signals such as read and write. (iii) A serial port sends data one bit at a time; a parallel port sends several bits at once over separate lines. (iv) The linker joins program parts into one executable program; the loader places that program into memory for running. (v) The CU (Control Unit) directs and controls all operations; the ALU performs arithmetic and logical operations.

7. Differentiate between Compiler and Interpreter.

A compiler translates the whole source program into machine code at once, producing an executable file; it is fast at run time, but errors are reported only after the whole translation. An interpreter translates and runs the program one statement at a time, stopping at the first error; it is slower at run time but easier for finding and correcting errors while learning and testing a program.

8. How to transfer data from CPU to memory? Explain in steps.

Data are transferred from the CPU to memory in these steps: (1) The CPU places the address of the memory location on the address bus. (2) It places the data to be stored on the data bus. (3) It sends a write signal on the control bus. (4) The memory unit reads the address and the write signal, and stores the data from the data bus into that location. (5) The memory sends back an acknowledgement, and the CPU continues with the next instruction.

9. Define the different types of RAM.

RAM (Random Access Memory) is the volatile main memory that holds data and programs while the computer is working. Its types are: DRAM (Dynamic RAM), which stores each bit as a charge that must be refreshed periodically; SRAM (Static RAM), which holds data as long as power is supplied and is faster but more expensive; and SDRAM (Synchronous DRAM), which works in step with the system clock and is used as the main memory of modern computers.

10. Define the general-purpose registers.

General-purpose registers are small, fast storage places inside the CPU that can hold data, addresses or results for any purpose during processing. Unlike special registers such as the program counter or accumulator, they are not fixed to one job: the programmer and the CPU use them freely for arithmetic, logical operations and temporary storage. Because they are inside the CPU, they are much faster than main memory.

11. Describe the Bus and its types.

A bus is a set of wires or lines that carries data, addresses and control signals between the parts of a computer. Its types are: the data bus, which carries the actual data; the address bus, which carries the address of the memory location or device; and the control bus, which carries control signals such as read, write and clock. Buses may be internal, inside the CPU, or external, joining the CPU to memory and devices.

12. Define the machine instructions.

Machine instructions are the binary-coded orders that the CPU can directly understand and execute. Each instruction has two parts: an operation code (opcode), which tells the CPU what operation to do, such as add, move or compare; and an operand, which gives the data or the address of the data to be used. Programs written in any language are finally translated into machine instructions before the CPU runs them.

13. Differentiate between Fetch instruction and Decode instruction.

The fetch step and the decode step are the first two stages of the CPU's instruction cycle. In the fetch step, the Control Unit takes the next instruction from memory, using the address in the program counter, and brings it into the instruction register. In the decode step, the Control Unit interprets (decodes) that instruction to find out which operation it orders and which data it needs, before the execute step carries it out.

14. Differentiate between ROM and RAM.

ROM (Read Only Memory) is non-volatile memory: it keeps its contents, such as the BIOS start-up program, even when the power is off, and it is normally only read, not written. RAM (Random Access Memory) is volatile memory: it holds the programs and data in current use, it can be both read and written, but its contents are lost when the power is switched off. ROM is small and permanent; RAM is large and temporary.

A computer virus is a harmful program, written by a person, that attaches itself to other programs or files and spreads from one computer to another, usually without the user's knowledge. When the infected program runs, the virus also runs, copies itself, and may damage data, slow down the system or stop it from working. Viruses spread through infected disks, downloads, e-mail attachments and networks.

5. Define the anti-virus software.

Anti-virus software, also called a vaccine, is a special program that detects, prevents and removes viruses from a computer. It scans files, disks and incoming e-mail, compares programs with a list of known viruses, and cleans or deletes infected files. To stay effective, anti-virus software must be updated regularly, because new viruses appear all the time.

6. How viruses may damage computer system?

Viruses damage a computer system by corrupting or deleting files and programs, changing data, filling up memory and disk space, and slowing down or stopping the system. Some viruses display annoying messages, while others steal or destroy important information and make the computer unusable. The damage begins when the virus activates, which may be at once or when a particular date or action triggers it.

7. Define Data protection and Piracy acts.

Data protection means the rules and techniques, such as passwords, audit checks and separation of duties, that keep data safe from loss, misuse and unauthorised access. Piracy acts are the laws that make it a crime to make or use illegal copies of copyrighted software. For example, the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act of 1984 defines software piracy as a crime, and copyright law protects software as the property of the person who developed it.

8. Describe the Legislation and Copyright Issues.

Legislation and copyright issues concern the legal protection of software and data. Software is the property of its developer, and a licence gives the buyer only the right to use it, not to copy or sell it. Making illegal copies is piracy and is punishable by law. Copyright law also covers books, music and films, and special laws, such as the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act of 1984, define computer crimes and their punishments.

9. Define the types of viruses.

The main types of viruses are: the boot sector virus, which infects the start-up part of a disk; the file virus, which attaches itself to program files; the worm, which copies and replicates itself across a network; the Trojan horse, which hides inside a harmless-looking program; the logic bomb, which activates on a particular event or date; and the macro virus, which spreads through documents such as word-processor files.

10. What is a password?

A password is a secret word or set of numbers that a user must type on the keyboard before an activity, such as logging into a computer or an account, can take place. It proves the user's identity and stops unauthorised persons from using the system or reading private data. A good password is kept secret, is hard to guess, and is changed regularly.

11. Write the names and define briefly the antivirus.

Common anti-virus programs (vaccines) are used to find and remove viruses: they scan the whole system, check new files and e-mail, and clean or quarantine infected items. Examples named in the chapter's era include Norton AntiVirus and McAfee VirusScan. Whichever program is used, it must be updated often with new virus definitions, because it can only recognise the viruses it knows.

12. Describe the exemption of 1990 act.

The exemption of the 1990 act refers to the legal exception that allows a lawful owner of software to make one copy of it for backup purposes. If the original disk is damaged or lost, the backup copy may be used instead, but it may not be sold, lent or given to others. This exemption protects the buyer against loss while still protecting the developer's copyright.

lessons.notes_html:
4. Define operating system and discuss their types.

An operating system is the system software that manages the computer's hardware and lets the user run programs. Its types are: single-user operating systems, used by one person at a time; multi-user operating systems, which let many users work at the same time; multitasking operating systems, which run several programs at once; multiprocessing operating systems, which use more than one processor; and command-line and graphical (GUI) operating systems, which differ in how the user gives commands.

5. Give a comparison between Command Line operating system and Graphical User Interface.

A command line operating system takes orders typed as text commands; it is fast and uses little memory, but the user must remember commands and typing mistakes cause errors. A graphical user interface (GUI) gives orders by clicking icons, menus and windows with a mouse; it is easier to learn and use, shows pictures and colours, but it needs more memory and a faster computer. Modern systems such as Windows use a GUI.

6. Discuss different features of Windows 2000 operating system.

Windows 2000 is a graphical operating system with a desktop, icons, windows, menus and a taskbar. Its features are: multitasking and multi-user working; plug and play, which detects and configures new devices automatically; Windows Explorer for managing files and folders; Disk Management for partitioning disks; a print queue for printing jobs; a Recycle Bin for deleted items; and network support for sharing files and printers.

7. Write a short note on each of the following: Disk Management Utility, Windows Explorer, Print Queue.

Disk Management Utility: a Windows tool that shows disks and partitions with a graphical interface, lets the user create and format partitions, and indicates which drive holds the system partition. Windows Explorer: a tool that displays folders and drives in a tree view and is used to navigate, copy, move, rename and delete files and folders. Print Queue: the waiting list Windows maintains for all printing jobs, so that documents are printed one after another in order.

8. What do you mean by Plug and Play? Does Windows 2000 provide this feature?

Plug and Play means that when a new device is connected, the computer automatically detects it and configures it, without the user having to set switches or install drivers by hand. Yes, Windows 2000 provides Plug and Play: on detecting a new device it finds the right driver, assigns resources to it, and makes it ready for use.

9. Define Partitioning. Briefly describe primary and extended partitioning.

Partitioning means dividing a hard disk into separate parts, called partitions, so that each part can be used as if it were a separate disk. A primary partition is a main partition that can hold an operating system and be booted from; at most four primary partitions can be created on a basic disk. An extended partition is a portion of a disk that can contain other (logical) partitions, so that more than four drives can be made on one disk.

10. Differentiate the following: Multitasking and Multiprocessing; File Management and Disk Management; Single-User operating system and Multi-User operating system.

Multitasking means one processor runs several programs by switching quickly between them; multiprocessing means two or more processors work together at the same time. File Management organises files and folders and controls access to them; Disk Management organises the disk itself, its partitions and formatting. A single-user operating system serves one user at a time; a multi-user operating system lets several users work on the same computer at the same time.

4. Write a note on the following: Word processor, Clipboard, Word Art.

Word processor: an application software that creates, edits, formats and prints text documents, with tools for fonts, margins, tables, pictures and spelling check; MS Word is an example. Clipboard: a temporary holding place in the computer's memory where data that is cut or copied is kept, so that it can be pasted into the same or another document. Word Art: a feature that creates decorative, coloured and shaped text for headings and titles, launched from the Drawing toolbar.

5. What is a text editor? Describe its basic features.

A text editor is a simple program used to create and edit plain text files without formatting such as fonts and pictures. Its basic features are: typing and deleting text; moving the cursor and scrolling; cut, copy and paste; find and replace; and saving and opening text files. Notepad is a common example. A text editor is used for notes and for writing program code.

6. Describe features of a full-featured word processor.

A full-featured word processor provides: WYSIWYG display, so the screen shows the document as it will print; fonts, sizes, colours and styles; paragraph formatting, alignment, line spacing and indents; headers, footers, footnotes and page numbers; tables, pictures, Word Art and charts; spelling and grammar check with a thesaurus; mail merge; and print preview with page setup for portrait or landscape pages.

7. Define font and discuss its types.

A font is the appearance or shape of a set of characters: its design, size and style. Font types are: serif fonts, which have small decorative lines at the ends of the strokes; sans-serif fonts, which have no such lines and look plain; and decorative or script fonts, which imitate handwriting or display lettering. Fonts are also described by size in points and by styles such as bold, italic and underline.

8. Describe formatting features for paragraph formatting.

Paragraph formatting controls how a paragraph looks on the page. 4. Define spreadsheet and discuss its basic features.

A spreadsheet is a software for manipulating numbers, arranged in a grid of rows and columns whose intersections form cells. Its basic features are: entering labels (text) and values (numbers); built-in formulas and functions for calculations; relative and absolute cell referencing; formatting of numbers, fonts and borders; charts such as pie charts; sorting and printing; and page setup with margins, headers and footers. MS Excel is the best-known spreadsheet.

5. Differentiate the following: Workbook and Worksheet; Active Cell and Passive Cell; Word Processor and Spreadsheet; Function and formula; Labels and Values.

Workbook and Worksheet: a workbook is a file that may contain many worksheets; a worksheet is one page (grid) inside it. Active Cell and Passive Cell: the active cell is the selected cell, shown by a bold border, ready for entry; other cells are passive. Word Processor and Spreadsheet: a word processor handles text documents, a spreadsheet handles numbers and calculations. Function and formula: a function is a built-in ready formula such as SUM(); a formula is an expression the user writes, such as =A1+B1. Labels and Values: labels are text that identify data; values are numbers on which calculations are done.

6. Every cell in a worksheet has a reference number, how is it calculated? Discuss with examples the major differences between Relative and Absolute referencing.

A cell's reference is its column letter followed by its row number, for example A1, B5 or C10. In relative referencing, the reference changes when a formula is copied: copying =A1+B1 from C1 to C2 gives =A2+B2, because the references move with the new position. In absolute referencing, dollar signs fix the reference, for example $A$1, so copying the formula anywhere still points to A1. Mixed referencing fixes only the row or only the column, such as A$1 or $A1.

7. Create a Pie chart for the marks obtained by your class fellows in SSC examination. [Practical task]

Practical task: enter your class fellows' names and their SSC marks in two columns of a worksheet, select the data, and use the Chart Wizard to insert a Pie chart, which shows each student's share of the total as a slice of a circle. Give the chart a title, label each slice with the student's name, and check that the slices add up to the whole class. Your own class data must be used.

8. What do you understand by the term name ranges? Can it be helpful in simplifying the worksheet?

Name ranges (named ranges) are names that the user defines to represent a cell or a range of cells on a worksheet, for example naming B2:B10 as 'Marks'. Yes, they simplify the worksheet: formulas become easy to read, such as =SUM(Marks) instead of =SUM(B2:B10), and mistakes are reduced, because the name stays correct even if rows or columns are added inside the range.

9. What are the advantages of using a spreadsheet program?

A spreadsheet program is fast and accurate: it recalculates all results at once when a number changes, so there is no need to redo long calculations by hand. It organises data in rows and columns, applies the same formula to many cells, draws charts from data, sorts and filters records, and prints neat tables. These advantages make it useful for accounts, results, budgets, stock and scientific data.

10. Insert another worksheet in the workbook of Q.4 to develop a Pie chart for the marks obtained by the students of your neighboring section in SSC examination. Calculate overall pass percentage, and average marks of the students of both sections in another (third) worksheet. [Practical task]

Practical task: keep the first section's data and pie chart in Sheet1, enter the neighbouring section's data in Sheet2 and make its pie chart the same way, then in Sheet3 link the two sheets to calculate the combined results. Overall pass percentage = (total passed students in both sections divided by total students in both sections) multiplied by 100. Average marks = (sum of all marks in both sections) divided by (total number of students). Use formulas that pick the data from Sheet1 and Sheet2, so the results update if the marks change.

4. Briefly describe the history of the Internet.

The internet began as ARPANET, a wide area network set up for a small number of users to share research between computers. Later the NSF established a separate high-speed network called NSFnet, and other networks joined, so the system grew into a world-wide network of networks. In 1989 the World Wide Web was established, giving easy, linked access to documents, and the internet then spread to homes, schools, offices and businesses everywhere.

5. Write a note on World Wide Web.

The World Wide Web (WWW) is the system of linked web pages on the internet, established in 1989. A collection of related web pages is called a web site, held on a web server and viewed with a web browser. Pages are written in HTML (Hyper Text Markup Language) and are reached by their address (URL), and they are linked by hyperlinks, so a reader can jump from one page to another. The Web is used for information, education, business and entertainment.

6. What do we mean by Addressing schemes? How many types of addressing is used on the Internet? Discuss briefly.

Addressing schemes are the systems used to identify computers and resources on the internet so that data reach the right place. Two main types are used: IP addresses and DNS addresses. An IP address is a 32-bit numeric address, written as four numbers called octets, for example 192.168.1.1. A DNS (Domain Name System) address is the easy-to-remember name form, such as www.example.com, which the system translates into the matching IP address.

7. What do you know about Email? Discuss briefly.

E-mail (electronic mail) is the exchange of messages over the internet. To send and receive e-mail, a user needs an e-mail account on an e-mail server and an e-mail address, written as user name @ DNS address, for example name@example.com. Messages are composed in an e-mail client such as Outlook Express, sent through the server, and stored in the receiver's mailbox until read. Files can be attached to messages, and unwanted junk mail is called spam.

8. Write a note on the following: Newsgroups, Search Engine, TCP/IP.

Newsgroups: discussion groups on the internet, classified by subject, where participants post messages for others to read and reply to; articles are exchanged between news servers using NNTP (Network News Transfer Protocol). Search Engine: a program, such as Google, that searches the Web for information on a topic and lists matching pages. TCP/IP: Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol, the basic set of rules of the internet; IP addresses and routes the data, and TCP breaks it into packets, checks them and puts them back in order.

9. Discuss limitations on email.

E-mail has several limitations: the sender may not know the person he is communicating with, because messages are only text and can give a wrong impression, and some people misrepresent themselves. Messages can be delayed, lost or blocked, and mailboxes can be filled with spam. Attachments may carry viruses, private mail can be read if it is not protected, and e-mail cannot carry the tone of voice or expressions of face-to-face talk.

10. How the use of Internet is affecting our society? Give your comments.

The internet is changing society in good and bad ways. It gives instant access to information, education, jobs, shopping, banking and contact with people anywhere, and it helps businesses and governments work faster. On the other hand, it spreads false information, wastes time, weakens privacy, and can harm health and social life when used too much. Used wisely, with care for truth, safety and balance, the internet is a great benefit to society.

mcqs.q: The internet began as ARPANET, which was set up to:
options: Share research between computers for a small number of users
mcqs.why: The internet began as ARPANET, a wide area network set up for a small number of users to share research between computers.

mcqs.q: The World Wide Web was established in which year?
mcqs.why: The World Wide Web was established in 1989, giving easy, linked access to documents on the internet.

mcqs.q: An IP address is a 32-bit numeric address written as four numbers called:
mcqs.why: An IP address is a 32-bit numeric address written as four numbers called octets, for example 192.168.1.1.

mcqs.q: A DNS address is the:
options: Easy-to-remember name form, such as www.example.com
mcqs.why: A DNS (Domain Name System) address is the easy-to-remember name form, which the system translates into the matching IP address.

mcqs.q: An e-mail address is written in the form:
mcqs.why: An e-mail address is written as user name @ DNS address, for example name@example.com, as the notes state.

mcqs.q: Unwanted junk mail received by e-mail is called:
mcqs.why: Unwanted junk mail is called spam, as stated in the notes on e-mail.

mcqs.q: Newsgroup articles are exchanged between news servers using:
mcqs.why: Newsgroups are discussion groups whose articles are exchanged between news servers using NNTP (Network News Transfer Protocol).

mcqs.q: In TCP/IP, the job of TCP is to:
options: Break data into packets, check them and put them back in order
mcqs.why: TCP breaks data into packets, checks them and puts them back in order, while IP addresses and routes the data.

mcqs.q: A search engine, such as Google, is a program that:
options: Searches the Web for information on a topic and lists matching pages
mcqs.why: A search engine searches the Web for information on a topic and lists matching pages, as described in the notes.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a limitation of e-mail given in the notes?
options: Mailboxes can be filled with spam
mcqs.why: The notes list limitations of e-mail: messages can be delayed, lost or blocked, mailboxes can be filled with spam, and attachments may carry viruses.
